newsitem.title: JAPAN: Fischler sees higher grain set-aside, defends wheat exports.
newsitem.headline: Fischler sees higher grain set-aside, defends wheat exports.

text.p: European Union Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler said on Tuesday that the EU's grain set-aside rate for 1997/98 should be raised because of higher crop output in 1996.
Fischler also shrugged off U.S. criticism over the EU's wheat export subsidies, saying the EU was acting within the framework of world trade agreements.
"It's clearly necessary to increase the set-aside rate for the next marketing year," Fischler told reporters in Makuhari, Chiba, where an international food exhibition is being held this week.
"We stick to the GATT's rules and obligations. But we'd like to add that we have no interest in undermining world wheat prices (with export subsidies)," Fischler added.
The EU's grain output was expected to have reached a record 202 million tonnes in 1996, around 27 million tonnes higher than in 1995.
The EU last summer halved the cereals set-aside rate to five percent for the 1997 harvest after public stocks fell to the lowest level for many years and prices soared.

Fischler said last week in Brussels that EU grain production was increasing at an "alarming" rate, and added a choice would have to be made between either increasing set-aside rates or removing export refunds.
But Fischler also said it was still too early to propose a set-aside rate for 1997/98.
"The decision (on the set-aside rate) is usually made in July. So before we have firm estimates of the harvest we can't fix the set-aside rate," Fischler said.
On wheat exports, Fischler said the EU was not doing anything wrong.
"We use export subsidies as a flexible instrument," Fischler said, adding that the EU was acting within GATT rules.
The EU last year reintroduced wheat export subsidies, leading to calls from some U.S. groups for retaliatory measures.

The U.S. Agriculture Department's (USDA) general sales manager Chris Goldthwait said late last month that the EU's subsidy levels were too high and that the USDA did not accept its argument that subsidies were necessary.

U.S. Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman also voiced his frustration, saying that the U.S. export subsidy programme, the Export Enhancement Program, is his "big stick" and that Washington is prepared to use it to fight unfair competition.
